en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Saṅghādisesa Offenses
11. The Training Rule on Following Schism At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, Devadatta was striving for a schism in the Saṅgha, for a schism in the Wheel.
The bhikkhus said this:
“Devadatta speaks what is contrary to the Dhamma; Devadatta speaks what is contrary to the Vinaya.
How indeed can Devadatta strive for a schism in the Saṅgha, for a schism in the Wheel?”
When this was said, Kokālika, Kaṭamodakatissaka, Khaṇḍadeviyā-putta, and Samuddadatta said this to those bhikkhus:
"Venerable sirs, do not speak thus.
Devadatta speaks in accordance with the Dhamma; Devadatta speaks in accordance with the Vinaya."
“Devadatta speaks on our behalf, taking up our will and inclination; he knows our mind and speaks for us, and this is approved by us.
Those monks who were few in desires... [as before] ... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can these monks become followers of Devadatta as he strives to cause a schism in the Saṅgha, siding with a faction?”
Then those monks, having rebuked those following monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“… Is it true, monks, that there are monks who act as followers and partisans of Devadatta as he strives for a schism in the Saṅgha?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can those foolish men, monks, act as followers and partisans of Devadatta while he is striving to cause a schism in the Saṅgha?
This, monks, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“If there are one, two, or three monks who are followers of that very monk and who speak divisively, and they should say:
‘Venerable sirs, do not say anything at all to this monk.’”
‘This monk speaks in accordance with the Dhamma; this monk speaks in accordance with the Vinaya.
This monk expresses himself according to our own will and preference, knowing and not speaking falsely; this is acceptable to us.
Those monks should be addressed by the other monks as follows:
‘Venerable sirs, do not speak thus;
this monk is not one who speaks according to the Dhamma, nor is he one who speaks according to the Vinaya;
let it not be pleasing to you, venerable sirs, that there should be a schism in the Saṅgha.’
‘The Saṅgha is united with these venerable ones; for when the Saṅgha is united, living in harmony, without dispute, and following a single recitation, it dwells in comfort.

If those bhikkhus, being thus addressed by the bhikkhus, should persist as before, those bhikkhus are to be formally admonished by the bhikkhus up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that [position].
If, being admonished up to three times, they relinquish it, that is good.
If they do not relinquish it, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
"Of that very person" means of that monk who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha.
"Bhikkhus" means there are other bhikkhus.
"Followers" means...
Whatever view he has, whatever conviction he has, whatever preference he has— those [who follow him] also have that same view, that same conviction, and that same preference.
"Those who speak in factions" means they stand on his side for the sake of his praise.
“One or two or three” means there is one, or two, or three. They might say this:
“Venerable sirs, do not say anything at all to this bhikkhu; this bhikkhu speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, this bhikkhu speaks in accordance with the Vinaya.”
"This monk speaks on our behalf, taking up our desire and our preference; he knows it, he does not speak falsely, and this is acceptable to us.
"Those monks" refers to those monks who follow along.
"By the bhikkhus" means by other bhikkhus. Those who see or hear [it] should say to them:
"Venerable sirs, do not speak thus."
This monk is not one who speaks according to the Dhamma; this monk is not one who speaks according to the Vinaya.
May it not be pleasing to the venerable ones as well that there should be a schism in the Saṅgha.
Let the venerable ones be reconciled with the Saṅgha.
"For the Saṅgha, being united, living in harmony, and free from dispute, with a single recitation, dwells in comfort.
This should be said a second time and a third time.
If they relinquish it, that is well;
if they do not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Having heard [the admonition], if they do not speak [to relinquish it], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Those monks, having been drawn even into the midst of the Saṅgha, should be told:
"Venerable sirs, do not speak thus.
This monk is not one who speaks according to the Dhamma; this monk is not one who speaks according to the Vinaya."
"Venerable sirs, may you also approve of the schism in the Saṅgha.
Let the venerable ones be united with the Saṅgha;
for when the Saṅgha is united, living in harmony, without dispute, and following a single recitation, it dwells in comfort."
A second time she should be told.
A third time she should be told.
If she relinquishes [the matter], that is good.
If they do not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Those monks are to be formally admonished.
"And thus, monks, are they to be formally admonished:
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
Such-and-such monks and such-and-such monks are followers and partisans of the monk so-and-so who is striving for a schism in the Saṅgha.”
They do not relinquish that matter.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha formally admonish the monks named so-and-so and so-and-so for the sake of their relinquishing that matter.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.
The monks named so-and-so and so-and-so are followers and partisans of the monk named so-and-so who is striving for a schism in the Sangha;
they do not relinquish that matter."
The Saṅgha admonishes the monks named so-and-so and named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
Whichever venerable one approves of the admonition of the monks named so-and-so and named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
A second time I speak this matter...
A third time I speak this matter:
Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
The monks named so-and-so and so-and-so are followers and partisans of the monk named so-and-so who is striving for a schism in the Saṅgha.
They do not relinquish that matter.
The Saṅgha formally admonishes the monks named so-and-so and so-and-so for the sake of relinquishing that matter.
Whichever venerable one approves of the formal admonition of the monks named so-and-so and so-and-so for the sake of their relinquishing that matter, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The monks named so-and-so and so-and-so have been formally admonished by the Saṅgha for the sake of their relinquishing that matter.
"It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent.
Thus do I understand this.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the motion.
With two proclamations, there are thullaccaya offenses;
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
For those committing a *saṅghādisesa*, there is a *dukkaṭa* for the motion (*ñatti*), and with the two proclamations, the thullaccayas are resolved.
Two or three may be admonished together, but more than that should not be admonished.
It is a *saṅghādisesa*...
[as before] ...therefore it is called a *saṅghādisesa*.
If, regarding a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), one perceives it as a legitimate legal act and does not relinquish [the offense], there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
If, regarding a legitimate legal act, one is doubtful and does not relinquish it, there is an offense entailing suspension.
If, regarding a legitimate legal act, one perceives it as an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*) and does not relinquish it, there is an offense entailing suspension.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as a legitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one is uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense for those who do not admonish,
or for those who relinquish [the matter].
Of those who are insane,
of those whose minds are deranged,
and of those overwhelmed by pain.
"Regarding those who are first offenders.
The eleventh training rule concerning those who follow a schism is finished.
